newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD wants Kohl to stick to EMU timetable.
newsitem.headline: German SPD wants Kohl to stick to EMU timetable.

text.p: Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday urged Chancellor Helmut Kohl to stick to the timetable for European Monetary Union (EMU) even if Germany does not conform to the strictest interpretation of the entry criteria.

The Maastricht Treaty allows more leeway than the Kohl government pretends, and Germany should make use of that to ensure EMU starts as scheduled in 1999, SPD European affairs spokeswoman Heidemarie Wieczorek-Zeul said.

She said the SPD would introduce a motion in parliament urging Bonn to make the most of its room for manoeuvre and warning that any delay in the timetable would cause "clear political and economic damage".
The rule that EMU members have budget deficits no higher than three percent of gross domestic product is not part of the treaty itself, but a "reference value" contained in a protocol.
And the treaty explicitly allows leeway for states that exceed this value if they are within a close range.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has stated that "three percent" in the treaty means 3.0 percent. His own Christian Social Union party has passed a resolution endorsing this interpretation.
"Waigel's formulations improperly limit the room for manoeuvre laid down in the treaty," Wieczorek-Zeul said. "Three point zero does not stand with a zero in the treaty."

Wieczorek-Zeul presented a draft version of the party's motion which says "the realisation of the third stage of European economic and monetary union, including the timetable, in accordance with the treaty is of central importance."

Waigel is insistent that Germany's 1997 deficit will be 2.9 percent of economic output, but continued high unemployment is increasing government outlays while cutting tax revenues, intensifying doubts it can meet the target.
Wiecozorek-Zeul declined to specify an acceptable deficit level but stressed the important factor was that the economic data of EMU particpants was converging at similar levels.
The SPD parliamentary group will approve a final version of the motion on May 13 and it will form the centrepiece of a major debate on European policy two days later, Wieczorek-Zeul said.
"We've forced a debate on EMU becuase we believe it's a very strange situation at the moment, with the government looking on while everyone else is talking about the euro," she said.
